## Research question

**Do schools with similar test results give similar secondary-school advice? (inference)**

At the end of primary school, pupils receive advice on which secondary-school track to follow. This advice combines teacher judgment with results from the *doorstroomtoets*. We examine whether schools with similar test performance give similar advice, and whether this relationship differs with the socioeconomic composition of their pupils (*schoolweging*).

Our main audience is policymakers and the general public. We therefore aim to show differences in the percentage of pupils receiving HAVO-or-higher advice, rather than focusing on regression coefficients.

## Data Processing

After understanding the data and producing our AI_CONTEXT.md file with all the specifications of the datasets we start processing the data in order to work with it.

DUO suppresses counts below five for privacy (DUO, 2025a, 2025b). Rather than dropping these observations, which would remove information from many schools, we replace them with 2.5, the midpoint of the possible values (1–4).

To calculate HAVO+ advice, we combine the HAVO, HAVO/VWO, and VWO categories. HAVO/VWO counts fully because both tracks meet the HAVO threshold, whereas VMBO-GT/HAVO is excluded because it includes a lower track. We divide this total by the number of pupils receiving advice, excluding those for whom no advice was recorded (`ADVIES_NIET_MOGELIJK`).

```{r prepare-exploratory-data}

# the count columns are character ("<5" privacy suppression) -> numeric first
advice_cols <- c(
  "VSO", "PRO", "VMBO_B", "VMBO_B_K", "VMBO_K", "VMBO_K_GT", "VMBO_GT",
  "VMBO_GT_HAVO", "HAVO", "HAVO_VWO", "VWO"
)

# changing all "<5" values to 2.5
to_num <- function(x) {
  if_else(x == "<5", 2.5, suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)))
}

# Normalize advice headers before preparing either analysis dataset.
names(schooladviezen) <- gsub("\\u00a0", "", names(schooladviezen))

# School identifiers occupy different positions in the two source files.
adv_ids <- schooladviezen[, 3:4]
ref_ids <- referentieniveaus[, 2:3]

adv <- schooladviezen |>
  mutate(across(all_of(advice_cols), to_num)) |>
  mutate(
    n_advice = rowSums(across(all_of(advice_cols)), na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_havo_plus = 100 * (HAVO + HAVO_VWO + VWO) / n_advice
  )

# proportion of pupils reaching the reference level, averaged across
# maths (1S) and reading (2F) — removes school size as a confound
reference_data <- referentieniveaus |>
  mutate(
    inst = ref_ids[[1]],
    vest = ref_ids[[2]],
    tot_m = to_num(REKENEN_LAGER1F) + to_num(REKENEN_1F) +
      to_num(REKENEN_1S) + to_num(REKENEN_2F),
    tot_r = to_num(LV_LAGER1F) + to_num(LV_1F) + to_num(LV_2F),
    pct_m = 100 * to_num(REKENEN_1S) / tot_m,
    pct_r = 100 * to_num(LV_2F) / tot_r,
    pct_test = (pct_m + pct_r) / 2
  ) |>
  select(inst, vest, pct_test)

# maths and reading separately, only needed for the subject plot
subject_pct <- referentieniveaus |>
  transmute(
    inst = ref_ids[[1]],
    vest = ref_ids[[2]],
    maths = 100 * to_num(REKENEN_1S) /
      (to_num(REKENEN_LAGER1F) + to_num(REKENEN_1F) +
         to_num(REKENEN_1S) + to_num(REKENEN_2F)),
    reading = 100 * to_num(LV_2F) /
      (to_num(LV_LAGER1F) + to_num(LV_1F) + to_num(LV_2F))
  )

# One school-level dataset for both exploratory advice plots.
exploratory_data <- tibble(
  inst = adv_ids[[1]],
  vest = adv_ids[[2]],
  n_advice = adv$n_advice,
  pct_havo_plus = adv$pct_havo_plus
) |>
  inner_join(reference_data, by = c("inst", "vest")) |>
  inner_join(subject_pct, by = c("inst", "vest")) |>
  # schools without advice, or with missing counts, cannot get a percentage
  filter(n_advice > 0, !is.na(pct_havo_plus), !is.na(pct_test))


# Drop the 119 empty locations (0 students, no schoolweging)
sw <- schoolweging |>
  filter(!is.na(schoolweging))

```

### Exploring test results and school advice

To measure test performance, we used the percentage of students reaching the target reference levels in maths (1S) and reading (2F), which are comparable across test providers (DUO, 2025a). Before combining them into one measure, we checked whether they showed similar relationships with HAVO+ advice, as averaging could otherwise hide important differences (Figure 1).

```{r exploratory-plot-subjects, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 6.5, fig.align = "center"}

# Dataframe with one row per school per subject
subject_data <- exploratory_data |>
  filter(!is.na(maths), !is.na(reading)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(maths, reading), names_to = "subject", values_to = "pct_target"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = if_else(subject == "maths", "Maths (1S)", "Reading (2F)"))

# Compare maths and reading against HAVO+ advice
subject_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = pct_target, y = pct_havo_plus, colour = label, fill = label)
  ) +
  # shape 21 is a filled circle, so the points use the fill colours
  geom_point(shape = 21, stroke = 0, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.3) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
    alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1.3
  ) +
  # light colours for the points, darker shades of the same for the lines
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#009E73", "#CC79A7"), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#00553E", "#7A2E5C"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 25)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100), expand = FALSE) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2.5))) +
  labs(
    title = "Schools whose students reach target levels give more HAVO+ advice",
    subtitle = "Each dot is one school; maths and reading shown separately",
    x = "% of students reaching the target level",
    y = "% of students advised HAVO or higher",
    caption = paste0(
      "Data: DUO, school year 2024–2025. ",
      "Lines: linear fit with 95% interval."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")


# correlation and slope per subject on school advice
subject_data |>
  group_by(subject) |>
  summarise(
    r = cor(pct_target, pct_havo_plus),
    slope = coef(lm(pct_havo_plus ~ pct_target))[2]
  )
```

Figure 1 shows similar relationships for maths and reading (both r = 0.61), suggesting that neither subject has a substantially stronger association with HAVO+ advice. We therefore averaged the two percentages into one test-performance measure for the remaining analysis.

```{r exploratory-plot-average, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 6.5, fig.align = "center"}

# Share receiving HAVO+ advice versus average reference-level attainment
# Plot advice against average test performance
exploratory_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_test, y = pct_havo_plus)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1, color = "#2878CC") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "#EB6734", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Schools with better test results give more HAVO+ advice",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Each dot is one school. Schools with similar test results ",
      "can still differ widely in their advice."
    ),
    x = paste0(
      "% of students reaching the target level ",
      "(average of maths 1S and reading 2F)"
    ),
    y = "% of students advised HAVO or higher",
    caption = paste0(
      "Data: DUO, school year 2024–2025. Regular primary schools only. ",
      "Line: linear fit with 95% interval."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey50", hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# linear model: how much HAVO+ advice changes per point of test results
fit_ref <- lm(pct_havo_plus ~ pct_test, data = exploratory_data)
summary(fit_ref)

```

Figure 2 shows a strong positive relationship between test performance and HAVO+ advice across 5,921 schools (r = 0.69). A 10-percentage-point increase in test performance was associated with approximately 7.6 percentage points more HAVO+ advice (b = 0.76).

However, test performance explained only 48% of the variation in advice (R² = 0.48), with substantial variation remaining around the fitted line (residual SE = 11.6 percentage points). This led us to investigate whether school disadvantage could help explain these differences.

### Exploring school weighting

We chose to investigate schoolweging, a measure of the socioeconomic disadvantage of a school's student population, where higher values indicate greater disadvantage. Rather than examining whether disadvantage is simply associated with higher or lower advice, we wanted to see whether it changes the relationship between test performance and HAVO+ advice.


```{r exploratory-plot-weighting, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6, fig.align = "center"}

sw_median <- median(sw$schoolweging)

sw |>
  ggplot(aes(x = schoolweging)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#2878CC", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_density(fill = "#2878CC", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = sw_median,
    linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = sw_median + 0.5,
    y = max(table(cut(sw$schoolweging, breaks = 40))) * 0.85,
    label = paste0("median = ", round(sw_median, 1)),
    hjust = 0, size = 3.5, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 40, by = 5)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(18, 43)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of school weighting",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Each school gets one score; higher = more disadvantaged ",
      "student population"
    ),
    x = "School weighting",
    y = "Number of schools",
    caption = "Data: Inspectorate of Education / CBS, school year 2024–2025"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Figure 3 shows that school weighting is continuously distributed around a median of approximately 29.5, without a clear cutoff between more and less disadvantaged schools. We therefore kept it continuous in our moderation model rather than dividing schools into categories.

## Moderation analysis

### Prepare the analysis data

For the moderation analysis, we combined the advice and test-performance data with school weighting. However, the school-weighting file uses different location identifiers, so we could only match schools by their main school code. For schools with multiple locations, we assigned the weighting of the first listed location to all of them.

This affected 305 of 5,873 locations. Although the median difference in weighting between locations of the same school was only 2.2 points, some differed by as much as 14.7. The assigned weighting may therefore be inaccurate for some locations. Schools without weighting data were excluded.

```{r prepare-moderation-data}

# Getting the advice data
# ==> Look at this Matheus
advice_data <- schooladviezen |>
  mutate(
    inst = adv_ids[[1]],
    vest = adv_ids[[2]],
    across(all_of(advice_cols), to_num),
    n_advice = rowSums(across(all_of(advice_cols)), na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_havo_plus = 100 * (HAVO +  HAVO_VWO + VWO) / n_advice
  ) |>
  filter(n_advice > 0) |>
  select(inst, vest, pct_havo_plus)
# ==>

# School weighting data
weighting_data <- schoolweging |>
  transmute(
    inst = sub("\\|.*$", "", OVT),
    schoolweging
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(schoolweging)) |>
  distinct(inst, .keep_all = TRUE)

# how many schools in the model data are affected by the data processing choice
multi_location <- schoolweging |>
  filter(!is.na(schoolweging)) |>
  count(inst = sub("\\|.*$", "", OVT)) |>
  filter(n > 1)

# how much do locations of the same school differ in school weighting?
schoolweging |>
  filter(!is.na(schoolweging)) |>
  mutate(inst = sub("\\|.*$", "", OVT)) |>
  group_by(inst) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(spread = max(schoolweging) - min(schoolweging)) |>
  summarise(median_spread = median(spread), max_spread = max(spread))

# The final model data
model_data <- advice_data |>
  inner_join(reference_data, by = c("inst", "vest")) |>
  inner_join(weighting_data, by = "inst") |>
  filter(!is.na(pct_test), !is.na(pct_havo_plus))


cat("Number of rows in the moderation dataframe:", n_distinct(model_data))

cat("School locations in the model affected by the first-location choice:",
    sum(model_data$inst %in% multi_location$inst), "of", nrow(model_data))

head(model_data)
```

### Model school disadvantage as a moderator

We fitted a linear regression with an interaction between test performance and school weighting. As discussed earlier, this allows us to examine whether the relationship between test results and advice changes depending on how disadvantaged a school's student population is.

```{r moderation-model}
model_havo <- lm(pct_havo_plus ~ pct_test * schoolweging, data = model_data)

model_results <- tibble(
  r_squared = summary(model_havo)$r.squared,
  interaction = coef(model_havo)[["pct_test:schoolweging"]]
)

model_results
```

The model explained approximately 53% of the variation in HAVO+ advice (R² = 0.58). The negative interaction (b = −0.035) indicates that the relationship between test performance and HAVO+ advice becomes weaker as disadvantage increases. In other words, advice increases more slowly with test performance in more disadvantaged schools.

#### Representative predictions

To make this interaction easier to interpret, we calculated predictions at the 25th and 75th percentiles of school weighting (27.4 and 31.8). These represent relatively lower and higher disadvantage without relying on extreme values. School weighting remains continuous in the model.

```{r moderation-predictions}
sw_values <- quantile(
  model_data$schoolweging,
  probs = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

```

```{r moderation-gap-check}
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    disadvantage_group = case_when(
      schoolweging <= sw_values[[1]] ~ "Lower disadvantage",
      schoolweging >= sw_values[[3]] ~ "Higher disadvantage",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    disadvantage_group = factor(
      disadvantage_group,
      levels = c("Lower disadvantage", "Higher disadvantage")
    )
  )

# Extend the fitted lines without changing the observed data.
x_line <- seq(10, 90, length.out = 200)

prediction_interactive <- expand_grid(
  pct_test = x_line,
  disadvantage = c("Lower disadvantage", "Higher disadvantage")
) |>
  mutate(
    schoolweging = if_else(
      disadvantage == "Lower disadvantage",
      as.numeric(sw_values[[1]]),
      as.numeric(sw_values[[3]])
    ),
    fit = predict(model_havo, newdata = pick(everything()))
  )

prediction_interactive <- prediction_interactive |>
  group_by(pct_test) |>
  mutate(
    difference_high = fit - fit[disadvantage == "Higher disadvantage"]
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", disadvantage, "</b>",
      "<br><br>Test performance: ", round(pct_test, 1), "%",
      "<br>Predicted HAVO+ advice: ", round(fit, 1), "%",
      "<br><br><b>Compared with higher-disadvantage schools:</b>",
      "<br><b>",
      if_else(
        abs(difference_high) < 1e-8,
        "Reference group",
        paste0(
          if_else(difference_high > 0, "+", ""),
          round(difference_high, 1),
          " percentage points"
        )
      ),
      "</b>"
    )
  )

gap_70 <- predict(
  model_havo,
  newdata = tibble(
    pct_test = 70,
    schoolweging = as.numeric(sw_values[c(1, 3)])
  )
) |>
  diff() |>
  abs() |>
  round(1)

overall_model <- lm(pct_havo_plus ~ pct_test, data = model_data)

overall_data <- tibble(pct_test = x_line) |>
  mutate(fit = predict(overall_model, newdata = pick(everything())))

overall_model
overall_data
```

At 70% test attainment, the model predicts approximately 56% HAVO+ advice at lower disadvantage, compared with 47% at higher disadvantage. This 9-percentage-point gap illustrates our main finding: schools with similar test results can give different proportions of HAVO+ advice, with the predicted gap widening at higher performance levels.

### Interactive visualization

We designed the interactive visualization to make the moderation results understandable without relying on regression coefficients. It initially shows the overall relationship between test performance and HAVO+ advice. Readers can then switch to predictions for lower and higher school disadvantage to see how the relationship changes.

We chose two representative lines to make the difference clear without overcrowding the graph. Individual schools remain visible to show the variation around the predictions, while highlighting the lowest and highest quarters of school weighting helps readers connect the model to the observed data.

Finally, hover labels show predicted HAVO+ advice and its difference from the higher-disadvantage reference in percentage points, making the comparison easier to interpret.

```{r interactive-data}

  "<br>But does this relationship hold equally across schools?"
)

subtitle_gap <- paste0(
  "At schools where 70% of pupils reach the target level,",
  "<br><b>about ", round(gap_70), " fewer pupils per 100</b> ",
  "are predicted to receive HAVO+ advice",
  "<br>in <span style='color:", group_colors[["Higher disadvantage"]],
  "'><b>higher-disadvantage schools</b></span> than in ",

)

footnote_2 <- paste0(
  "<b>Source:</b> DUO, school year 2024-2025; ",
  "schoolweging (2022-2025).",
  "<br><b>Authors:</b> Matheus Nacif, Ilinca Anton, Isabella Braune."
)

interactive_plot <- plot_ly(height = 850)

# Default state: all schools
interactive_plot <- interactive_plot |>
  add_markers(
    data = model_data,
    x = ~pct_test,
    y = ~pct_havo_plus,

    hoverinfo = "skip",

# Lower- and higher-disadvantage dots
for (group in c("Lower disadvantage", "Higher disadvantage")) {

  interactive_plot <- interactive_plot |>

      legendgroup = group
    )
}

# Overall fitted relationship
interactive_plot <- interactive_plot |>
  add_lines(
    data = overall_data,
    x = ~pct_test,

    line = list(color = group_sec_text, width = 5),

      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

# Lower- and higher-disadvantage predictions
for (group in c("Lower disadvantage", "Higher disadvantage")) {
  line_data <- prediction_interactive |>
    filter(disadvantage == group)

  interactive_plot <- interactive_plot |>
    add_lines(
      data = line_data,

              list(
                visible = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
              ),
              list(
                showlegend = TRUE,
                "annotations[1].text" = subtitle_gap
              )
            )
          )
        )
      )
    )
  )

interactive_plot |> theme_interactive()
```

### Conclusion

Our results suggest that school disadvantage is associated with how closely secondary-school advice follows test performance. Although schools with better test results generally give more HAVO+ advice, this relationship is weaker in more disadvantaged schools. The difference is particularly noticeable at higher levels of test performance.

However, these are school-level comparisons. We cannot conclude that individual pupils with identical test results receive different advice because of their socioeconomic background. Other differences between schools may also contribute to the pattern, especially considering the differences in test providers and how these are interpreted, which is an important debate now.

Nevertheless, the analysis shows that test performance alone does not fully explain differences in secondary-school advice, and that school disadvantage is relevant to understanding them.
